terms.def: Information gathered directly with your senses or with instruments.
sents: “The sandstone layer is 12 cm thick” is an _____.
A thermometer reading is still an _____, even though an instrument made it.
Ripple marks on top of a rock layer are an _____; saying a lake once covered the area is an inference.

terms.def: An explanation of observations that goes beyond what was directly observed.
sents: “This layer formed at the bottom of a lake” is an _____.
Words such as because, must have and probably usually signal an _____.
More than one _____ can fit the same set of observations.

terms.def: A statement of what you expect to observe, based on a pattern, model, or hypothesis.
sents: Using the pattern in past readings, the student made a _____ that the pressure would keep falling.
A hypothesis is tested by checking whether its _____ matches new observations.

terms.def: A possible explanation that can be tested with observations or experiments.
sents: Before collecting shadow data, each group wrote a _____ that the data could test.
A _____ must be testable; if no observation could ever show it is wrong, it is not scientific.

terms.def: A well-tested explanation supported by many lines of evidence.
terms.every: a guess or hunch (“I have a theory about who ate my lunch”)
sents: Plate tectonics is a _____: it explains earthquakes, volcanoes and mountain belts and is backed by many lines of evidence.
A _____ explains why something happens; it never “grows up” into a law.

terms.def: A description of a pattern in nature that holds under stated conditions, often written as an equation.
terms.every: a rule that people must obey
sents: A scientific _____ describes what happens; a theory explains why.
A scientific _____ is often written as an equation that holds under stated conditions.

terms.def: A simplified representation of a real system: a diagram, physical model, equation, or computer simulation.
terms.every: a person who poses for photos, or a small toy copy
sents: The Model of Earth’s Interior Structure on ESSRT page 11 is a _____: useful, but it leaves things out.
A classroom globe is a _____ of Earth.
Every _____ leaves something out of the real system it represents.

terms.def: Observations and data used to support or refute a claim.
sents: In a CER, the _____ is the specific numbers, locations or features that back up the claim.
Photographs from space are the most direct _____ of Earth’s shape.

terms.def: The amount of doubt in a measurement or conclusion. Every measurement has some, and more evidence reduces it.
terms.every: feeling unsure of yourself or of what to do
sents: Measuring the same pebble three times and getting three slightly different volumes shows the _____ in the measurement.
Gathering more evidence reduces _____.

terms.def: A direct answer to a question, in one complete sentence.
sents: The first part of a CER is the _____: a direct answer in one complete sentence.
“Earth is not a perfect sphere” is a _____ that needs evidence to back it up.

terms.def: The part of a CER that explains why the evidence supports the claim by connecting it to a science idea.
sents: Restating the evidence is not _____.
In a CER, the _____ links the data to a science idea, such as density.

terms.def: To show that a claim is wrong, using evidence.
sents: Use the scientific meaning of theory to _____ the statement “plate tectonics is just a guess.”
Evidence can support a claim or _____ it.

terms.def: Anything that has mass and takes up space.
terms.every: to be important (“it doesn’t matter”)
sents: Rocks, water and air are all _____: each has mass and takes up space.

terms.def: The amount of matter in an object, measured in grams with a balance. It does not change with location.
sents: An astronaut’s _____ is the same on the Moon as on Earth.
A balance measures _____ in grams.

terms.def: The pull of gravity on an object’s mass. It changes with location.
terms.every: often used to mean mass (“I weigh 60 kilograms”)
sents: An astronaut’s _____ is less on the Moon because the Moon’s gravity is weaker.
On Jupiter a bathroom scale would show a greater _____, even though your mass would not change.

terms.def: The amount of space an object takes up, measured in mL or cm³ (1 mL = 1 cm³).
terms.every: how loud a sound is
sents: For a regular solid, _____ = length × width × height.
The water rose from 30.0 mL to 38.5 mL, so the rock’s _____ is 8.5 mL.

terms.def: Finding an irregular object’s volume from how much the water level rises when the object is submerged.
sents: To find the volume of an oddly shaped pebble, use _____: final water level minus starting water level.

terms.def: How far a measurement is from the accepted value, as a percent of the accepted value.
sents: Measuring water’s density as 1.06 g/mL when the accepted value is 1.00 g/mL gives a _____ of 6%.
The accepted value goes in the denominator when you calculate _____.

terms.def: The best known value of a quantity, used as the standard to compare a measurement to.
sents: Earth’s equatorial diameter on ESSRT page 2 (12,756 km) is the _____ to compare your estimate to.

terms.def: How fast something changes: change in value ÷ change in time.
sents: Air pressure falling 48 mb in 16 hours is a _____ of 3.0 mb/h.
A _____ always has “per” in its unit.

terms.def: An equation showing that two ratios are equal, used to scale a model up or down.
sents: To find how tall Mt. Marcy should be on a 30 cm globe, set up a _____: model height ÷ real height = model diameter ÷ real diameter.

terms.def: A model in which every part is made smaller (or larger) by the same factor as the real thing.
sents: A register tape where 1 meter = 1 billion years is a _____ of Earth’s history.
In a _____ of Earth on a 30 cm globe, Mt. Marcy would be thinner than a pencil line.

terms.def: The variable that is changed or used to organize the data. It goes on the x-axis (often time).
sents: On a graph of global temperature by year, the year is the _____.

terms.def: The variable that responds or is measured. It goes on the y-axis.
sents: On a graph of snow depth over six days, snow depth is the _____.

terms.def: As x increases, y increases.
sents: On a mass-vs.-volume graph, mass increases as volume increases: a _____.

terms.def: As x increases, y decreases.
sents: As a storm’s strength increased, the air pressure at its center fell: an _____.
“As x increases, y decreases” describes an _____.

terms.def: A relationship in which y stays the same as x increases (also called static).
terms.every: happening all the time (“constant noise”)
sents: The density of quartz stays the same no matter how big the sample is, so density vs. sample size shows a _____ relationship.

terms.def: A pattern that repeats at regular intervals.
sents: Hours of daylight in Glen Head plotted over three years show a _____ pattern that repeats every year.

terms.def: A line showing the general trend of the data, with about as many points above it as below it.
sents: Do not connect the dots; draw a _____ instead.

terms.def: The difference between a measured value and a baseline average. Zero means equal to the average.
terms.every: something strange or out of place
sents: A temperature _____ of +1.2 °C means 1.2 °C warmer than the 1951–1980 average.
On an _____ graph, 0 means “equal to the average,” not “none.”

terms.def: The average used as the zero point on an anomaly graph.
sents: Before reading an anomaly graph, find the _____ in the title or caption; for GISTEMP it is 1951–1980.

terms.def: The amount of mass in a given volume of a substance: D = m/V, in g/cm³ or g/mL.
sents: A boulder and a pebble of the same mineral have the same _____.
Ice floats because its _____ is lower than liquid water’s.
Warm air rises because heating lowers its _____.

terms.def: To take up more volume.
sents: Heating makes a substance _____, so its density decreases.
Water is unusual because it will _____ when it freezes.

terms.def: To shrink into less volume.
terms.every: a signed agreement
sents: Cooling makes a substance _____, so its density increases.

terms.def: The physical form of a substance: solid, liquid, or gas.
terms.every: a stage you go through (“it’s just a phase”)
sents: Most substances are densest in their solid _____; water is the major exception.

terms.def: The steepness of a line on a graph: change in y ÷ change in x.
terms.every: a hill or ski run
sents: On a mass-vs.-volume graph, the _____ of each line is the substance’s density.

terms.def: The changing mixture of gases and small particles surrounding Earth, including water vapor, clouds and aerosols.
sents: Water vapor belongs to the _____, not the hydrosphere.
Storm winds during a nor’easter are evidence for the _____.

terms.def: Earth’s water in liquid and frozen forms: oceans, lakes, rivers, groundwater, glaciers and ice.
sents: A glacier in Alaska is part of the _____.
The ice on Lake Ronkonkoma is part of the _____.

terms.def: The solid parts of Earth: rocks, sediments, soils and landforms.
sents: Sand washed off a dune on Fire Island is evidence for the _____.
Soil is part of the _____, but the organisms living in it are part of the biosphere.

terms.def: All living things on Earth: life on land, in water, and microscopic life.
sents: Mussels growing on a dock in Long Island Sound are part of the _____.
Marsh grasses buried by storm sand are part of the _____.

terms.def: A set of parts that interact, so a change in one part causes changes in others.
sents: Scientists study the spheres separately, but they act as one _____: a change in one drives changes in the others.

terms.def: When changes in one system drive changes in another, and back again, over long stretches of time.
sents: Cyanobacteria added oxygen to the atmosphere, and the oxygen-rich atmosphere allowed new kinds of life: an example of _____.

terms.def: The event, 2.8–2.5 billion years ago, when oxygen from cyanobacteria combined with iron and formed iron-oxide layers on the ocean floor.
sents: Repeated iron-oxide layers on the ancient ocean floor formed during the _____ event, 2.8–2.5 billion years ago.

terms.def: The event, 2.4–2.1 billion years ago, when oxygen from the ocean escaped into Earth’s atmosphere.
sents: According to ESSRT page 6, the _____ began about 2.4 billion years ago, when oxygen escaped from the ocean into the air.

terms.def: Microscopic organisms that make food by photosynthesis and release oxygen.
sents: The first organisms to add large amounts of oxygen to Earth’s oceans were photosynthesizing _____.

terms.def: The largest division of geologic time (for example, the Phanerozoic).
sents: The Phanerozoic, the last 539 million years, is an _____.

terms.def: A division of an eon (for example, the Cenozoic).
terms.every: any time in history (“the disco era”)
sents: The Cenozoic, the time of mammals and humans, is an _____.

terms.def: A division of an era (for example, the Devonian).
terms.every: a dot at the end of a sentence, or a class period
sents: The Devonian, when Earth’s earliest forests grew at Gilboa, NY, is a geologic _____.
The Cambrian, when the first animals with hard shells appeared, is a geologic _____.

terms.def: A division of a period (for example, the Pleistocene).
sents: Humans appear only in the Pleistocene _____ row of ESSRT page 6.

terms.def: The first and longest part of Earth’s history, from about 4.6 billion to 539 million years ago.
sents: The left side of ESSRT page 6 shows the _____, measured in billions of years ago.

terms.def: The last 539 million years of Earth’s history, when complex life with hard parts became common.
sents: Only about 11.7% of Earth’s history falls in the _____.
The right side of ESSRT page 6 shows the _____, measured in millions of years ago.

terms.def: A fossil of an organism that lived over a wide area for only a short time, which makes it a marker of a specific time.
sents: An organism that lived across a wide area for only a short time makes a useful _____.
On ESSRT page 7, each _____ is labeled with a letter from A to BB.

terms.def: A layered rock mound built by mats of cyanobacteria; stromatolites are the oldest undisputed evidence of life (about 3.5 billion years).
sents: The oldest undisputed evidence of life, about 3.5 billion years old, is a layered mound called a _____.
Cryptozoon, index fossil A on ESSRT page 7, is a _____ found near Saratoga Springs, NY.

terms.def: Made of many cells.
sents: The first _____ life, the soft-bodied Ediacaran fauna, appeared about 635 million years ago.

terms.def: A sphere slightly flattened at the poles and bulging at the equator. Earth’s true shape.
sents: Because Earth rotates, it is an _____, slightly flattened at the poles.
Earth is an _____, but the flattening is so slight that a to-scale drawing is still a circle.

terms.def: The distance across a planet through its center at the equator.
sents: Earth’s _____ (12,756 km) is larger than its polar diameter (about 12,714 km).

terms.def: The distance across a planet through its center from pole to pole.
sents: In the roundness ratio, the _____ goes on top.

terms.def: The distance around a circle or sphere.
sents: Eratosthenes used shadows in two cities to calculate Earth’s _____.
Earth’s equatorial _____ is about 40,075 km.

terms.def: Polar diameter ÷ equatorial diameter. The closer to 1.000, the more spherical the object.
sents: Earth’s _____ is 0.997, so drawn to scale it looks like a perfect circle.

terms.def: Greek scholar who, about 240 BCE, calculated Earth’s circumference from the difference in Sun angle between two cities and the distance between them.
sents: Around 240 BCE, _____ calculated Earth’s circumference using shadows and the distance between two cities.

terms.def: Angular distance north or south of the equator, from 0° to 90°.
sents: In New York, the altitude of Polaris equals your _____.
Glen Head’s _____ is about 40°50′ N.

terms.def: Angular distance east or west of the Prime Meridian, from 0° to 180°.
sents: A ship whose solar time is 4 hours earlier than at the Prime Meridian is at 60° W _____.
Every 15° of _____ is about one hour of time difference.

terms.def: The line of 0° latitude, halfway between the North and South Poles.
sents: Latitude is measured north or south from the _____.
terms.parts: equa- (equal): splits Earth into equal halves

terms.def: The line of 0° longitude, passing through Greenwich, England.
sents: Longitude is measured east or west from the _____.

terms.def: A line of latitude. Parallels run east–west but measure distance north–south.
sents: The 41° N _____ runs east–west through Long Island.

terms.def: A line of longitude. Meridians run north–south and meet at the poles.
sents: Places on the same _____ have the same solar time.

terms.def: A location’s latitude and longitude, written latitude first with compass directions (40°50′ N, 73°37′ W).
sents: Glen Head’s _____ are about 40°50′ N, 73°37′ W.

terms.def: One-sixtieth of a degree: 1° = 60′.
terms.every: one-sixtieth of an hour
sents: 42°30′ is halfway between 42° and 43°, because each degree is divided into 60 _____s.

terms.def: The North Star, almost directly above Earth’s North Pole. Its altitude equals the observer’s latitude.
sents: From Glen Head, _____ appears about 41° above the northern horizon.
At the North Pole, _____ is directly overhead.

terms.def: A region about 15° of longitude wide that uses the same clock time.
sents: Because Earth rotates 15° per hour, each _____ is about 15° of longitude wide.

terms.def: Time set by the Sun’s position in the sky, which changes with longitude.
sents: Clock time is the same across a whole time zone, but _____ changes by 4 minutes for every degree of longitude.

terms.def: The part of a map that relates distance on the map to distance on the ground.
sents: To find the straight-line distance from Syracuse to Albany, compare your measurement to the _____ on ESSRT page 8.

terms.def: A model with a motionless Earth at the center and the Sun, Moon, planets and stars all moving around it.
sents: Ptolemy’s _____ placed a motionless Earth at the center of everything.
In the _____, the Sun travels around Earth once a day.

terms.def: A model with the Sun at the center and Earth as one of the planets moving around it.
sents: Copernicus published the _____ in 1543.
In the _____, retrograde motion happens naturally when Earth passes an outer planet.

terms.def: A small circle that Ptolemy added to a planet’s path to explain why planets sometimes appear to move backward.
sents: In Ptolemy’s model, each planet rode on an _____, a small circle carried along a larger one.

terms.def: The apparent shift of a nearby star against more distant stars as Earth moves to opposite sides of its orbit.
sents: Between January and July, a nearby star appears to shift against distant stars; this _____ is direct evidence that Earth revolves.
Astronomers first measured _____ in 1838.
The closer the star, the larger its _____.

terms.def: Astronomer in Alexandria who, about 150 CE, built the most successful geocentric model, used for more than 1,400 years.
sents: Around 150 CE, _____ built the geocentric model that astronomers used for more than 1,400 years.

terms.def: Polish astronomer who published the heliocentric model in 1543.
sents: In 1543, _____ published a model with the Sun at the center.

terms.def: Italian astronomer who, in 1610, used a telescope to observe moons orbiting Jupiter.
sents: In 1610, _____ saw moons orbiting Jupiter through a telescope, showing that not everything orbits Earth.

terms.def: Motion an object seems to have because the observer is moving.
terms.every: “apparent” meaning obvious (“it was apparent she was tired”)
sents: The Sun’s daily trip across the sky is _____ caused by Earth’s rotation.
Stars circling Polaris each night is an example of _____.

terms.def: Motion of the object itself.
sents: The Moon orbiting Earth is _____: the Moon itself is moving.

terms.def: The spinning of an object on its axis. Earth rotates west to east, 15° per hour.
sents: Earth’s _____ makes the Sun, Moon and stars appear to rise in the east and set in the west.
One _____ of Earth, measured from noon to noon, takes 24 hours.

terms.def: The imaginary line an object spins around. Earth’s axis runs through the North and South Poles.
terms.every: in math, the x-axis or y-axis of a graph
sents: Polaris lies almost directly above Earth’s _____, so it barely moves during the night.

terms.def: A star close enough to Polaris that it never sets, so it can be seen on every clear night.
sents: A _____ is close enough to Polaris that, from New York, it never sets.
The farther north you are, the more stars are a _____.

terms.def: An arc a star makes in a time-exposure photograph; each arc is centered on Polaris.
sents: In a photo where each _____ covers 75°, the camera’s shutter was open for 5 hours.

terms.def: A swinging pendulum whose direction of swing appears to turn because Earth rotates beneath it.
sents: At the North Pole, the swing of a _____ appears to turn 15° per hour.
A _____ shows that the ground itself is turning, not the sky.

terms.def: The apparent curving of winds, ocean currents and long flights: to the right in the Northern Hemisphere, to the left in the Southern Hemisphere.
sents: Because of the _____, winds in the Northern Hemisphere curve to the right.
The _____ is zero at the equator and greatest at the poles.

terms.def: The movement of one object around another along an orbit. Earth revolves around the Sun once every 365.26 days.
terms.every: overthrowing a government (the American Revolution)
sents: Earth’s _____ around the Sun makes different constellations visible in different seasons.
One _____ of Earth around the Sun takes 365.26 days (ESSRT page 2).

terms.def: The path of one object around another.
sents: Earth’s _____ around the Sun is an ellipse that is very nearly a circle.
A planet’s inertia and the Sun’s gravity together bend its path into an _____.

terms.def: A named pattern of stars in the sky.
sents: Orion is a winter _____ in New York, and Scorpius is a summer one.

terms.def: The ring of constellations that the Sun appears to pass in front of during the year.
sents: Each month the Sun appears in front of a different _____ constellation, drifting east about 1° per day.

terms.def: The time an object takes to spin once on its axis.
sents: Earth’s _____ on ESSRT page 2 is 23 h 56 min, measured against the stars.
Venus has the longest _____ of any planet: 243.7 days.

terms.def: The time an object takes to complete one orbit.
sents: On ESSRT page 2, Earth’s _____ is 365.26 days.
Mars has a _____ of 1.9 years.

terms.def: How wide an object appears in the sky, measured as an angle. It depends on the object’s actual size and its distance.
sents: The Sun’s _____ is largest in early January, when Earth is closest to it.
The Sun and Moon have about the same _____: the Sun is about 400 times wider but also about 400 times farther away.

terms.def: How flattened (out of round) an orbit is, from 0 for a perfect circle to almost 1 for a very flat ellipse.
sents: Earth’s orbit has an _____ of 0.017, so it is very nearly a circle.
Halley’s Comet’s orbit has an _____ of 0.967: a long, flat ellipse.
A higher _____ means a flatter orbit, not a bigger one.

terms.def: A short time when a planet appears to move westward against the background stars, opposite its usual eastward drift.
sents: When Earth passes Mars on the inside track, Mars appears to loop westward in _____.
Ptolemy’s epicycles were his way of explaining _____.

terms.def: An imaginary straight line from an observer to an object.
sents: As Earth passes Mars, our _____ to Mars swings backward against the distant stars.

terms.def: The yearly cycle of changes in temperature and hours of daylight, caused by Earth’s tilt, its revolution, and parallelism.
sents: Earth has _____ because its tilted axis keeps pointing the same direction as it revolves around the Sun.
A planet with no axial tilt would have no _____.

terms.def: The angle between a planet’s axis and a line perpendicular to its orbit. Earth’s is 23.44° (ESSRT page 2), rounded to 23.5°.
sents: Earth’s _____ is 23.5° every day of the year, including the equinoxes.
Mercury has almost no seasons caused by tilt because its _____ is only 0.03°.

terms.def: Earth’s axis always points in the same direction in space, toward Polaris.
sents: Because of _____, the Northern Hemisphere leans toward the Sun on one side of the orbit and away from it on the other.

terms.def: Sunlight that strikes the ground at 90°, so the Sun is directly overhead at solar noon.
terms.every: “direct” meaning straightforward (“a direct answer”)
sents: On June 21, the _____ strike the Tropic of Cancer, 23.5° N.
The _____ never reach New York; the farthest north they go is 23.5° N.

terms.def: The point in the sky directly above the observer (90° altitude).
sents: Where the direct rays strike, the Sun is at the _____ at solar noon.
For an observer at the North Pole, Polaris is at the _____.

terms.def: June 21, when the Northern Hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun and the direct rays strike the Tropic of Cancer.
sents: On the _____, the Sun’s path in Sea Cliff is the longest of the year, about 15 hours.

terms.def: December 21, when the Northern Hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun and the direct rays strike the Tropic of Capricorn.
sents: On the _____, the noon Sun in Sea Cliff is only 25.5° high.

terms.def: March 21 or September 23, when neither hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun and the direct rays strike the equator.
sents: On an _____, every place on Earth has 12 hours of daylight.
The Sun rises due east and sets due west only on an _____.

terms.def: The line of latitude at 23.5° N, the farthest north the direct rays reach (June 21).
sents: On June 21, the noon Sun is directly overhead on the _____.

terms.def: The line of latitude at 23.5° S, the farthest south the direct rays reach (December 21).
sents: On December 21, the direct rays strike the _____, 23.5° S.

terms.def: The region between 23.5° N and 23.5° S, the only latitudes where the Sun can ever be directly overhead.
sents: The Sun can be directly overhead only in _____, between 23.5° N and 23.5° S.

terms.def: The point in an orbit closest to the Sun. Earth reaches it around January 3.
sents: Earth is at _____, about 147 million km from the Sun, in early January, during New York’s winter.
A planet moves fastest at _____.

terms.def: The point in an orbit farthest from the Sun. Earth reaches it around July 4.
sents: Earth is at _____, about 152 million km from the Sun, in early July.
A planet moves slowest at _____.

terms.def: When one hemisphere has summer, the other has winter, because one is tilted toward the Sun while the other is tilted away.
sents: Summer in New York is winter in Argentina: the two hemispheres have _____.

terms.def: INcoming SOLar radiATION: the sunlight that reaches Earth.
sents: A low Sun spreads the same _____ over a larger area of ground.

terms.def: The angle between the ground and the Sun’s rays; 90° where the direct rays strike.
sents: During a day, the _____ is greatest at solar noon.
The farther a place is from the latitude of the direct rays, the lower its _____.

terms.def: How concentrated sunlight is on an area.
terms.every: how strong a feeling or effort is (“the intensity of the game”)
sents: As the angle of insolation decreases, the same beam spreads over more ground, so its _____ decreases.

terms.def: The number of hours of daylight.
sents: Sea Cliff has about 15 hours of daylight on June 21 and about 9 on December 21: a change in _____.

terms.def: The line that separates Earth’s day side from its night side.
sents: The _____ always divides the equator in half, so the equator has 12 hours of daylight every day.
On the equinoxes, the _____ passes through both poles.

terms.def: The line of latitude at 66.5° N. On June 21, the Sun does not set at or north of it.
sents: On June 21, the Sun does not set at or north of the _____.

terms.def: The line of latitude at 66.5° S. On December 21, the Sun does not set at or south of it.
sents: On December 21, the Sun does not set at or south of the _____.

terms.def: A model of the sky as a dome over the observer, used to show the Sun’s apparent path.
sents: The Sun’s apparent path is modeled on a _____, with the observer at the center.

terms.def: The compass direction of an object, measured clockwise from north (N = 0°, E = 90°, S = 180°, W = 270°).
sents: An object due south has an _____ of 180°.
On December 21, the Sun rises at an _____ of about 122° in Sea Cliff.

terms.def: The angle of an object above the horizon, from 0° at the horizon to 90° at the zenith.
terms.every: height above sea level (an airplane’s altitude)
sents: The noon Sun’s _____ in Sea Cliff is 72.5° on June 21.
The _____ of Polaris equals your latitude.

terms.def: Where the ground appears to meet the sky (0° altitude).
sents: Altitude is measured up from the _____.
At the equator, Polaris sits on the _____.

terms.def: The moment the Sun reaches its highest altitude of the day; in New York it is due south.
terms.every: “noon” meaning 12:00 on the clock
sents: At _____, the Sun is due south and shadows are the shortest of the day.

terms.def: Half of Earth. The equator divides it into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres.
sents: In the Southern _____, the noon Sun is due north and noon shadows point south.

terms.def: The Sun and everything held in orbit around it by its gravity: planets, dwarf planets, moons, asteroids, comets and dust.
sents: The Sun holds more than 99.8% of the mass of the _____.

terms.def: A huge ball of hot gas that gives off its own light, produced by nuclear fusion in its core.
terms.every: a famous person, or a five-pointed shape
sents: The Sun is the only _____ in our solar system.

terms.def: An object that orbits the Sun, has enough mass to pull itself round, and has cleared the area around its orbit.
sents: Pluto is round and orbits the Sun, but it is not a _____ because it has not cleared its orbit.
The word _____ comes from a Greek word meaning “wanderer.”

terms.def: An object that orbits the Sun and is round, but has not cleared its orbit and is not a moon.
sents: Ceres is in the asteroid belt, but it is a _____ because it is round.
Pluto and Eris are each a _____.

terms.def: An object that orbits a planet or a dwarf planet.
sents: Ganymede is a _____ of Jupiter, and it is wider than the planet Mercury.

terms.def: One of the four inner planets (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars): small and rocky, with metal cores and high densities.
sents: Mars is a _____: small, rocky and dense.

terms.def: One of the four outer planets (Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune): very large, mostly hydrogen and helium, with low densities, many moons and rings.
sents: Saturn is a _____: huge and low in density, with many moons and rings.

terms.def: A rocky or metallic object that orbits the Sun and is too small to be pulled into a round shape.
sents: Pallas, on ESSRT page 2, is a large _____, not a dwarf planet.

terms.def: The region between Mars and Jupiter where most asteroids orbit.
sents: Ceres orbits the Sun in the _____.
The _____ is material that never came together into a planet, not the remains of one that broke apart.

terms.def: A small body of ice, dust and rock on a long, very eccentric orbit. Near the Sun its ice turns to gas, forming a coma and tails.
sents: A _____’s tails always point away from the Sun.
Halley’s _____ has an orbital eccentricity of 0.967.

terms.def: The glowing cloud of gas around a comet’s center, formed when its ice turns to gas near the Sun.
